pull_request.title: perf(models): move to GLM 5.2, and make reasoning configurable
pull_request.body:
## What changed

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `scan` | `minimax/minimax-m3` | `z-ai/glm-5.2` |
| `deep` | `moonshotai/kimi-k3` | `z-ai/glm-5.2` |
| `fallback` | `kimi-k2.7-code`, `minimax-m2.1` | `deepseek-v4-pro`, `minimax-m3` |
| reasoning | hard-disabled | `high`, and configurable |

## Measured, not chosen from a rate card

Same prompt, same strict JSON schema, same 8000-token ceiling, three runs each:

| model | parses | avg cost/call | reasoning tokens | cached |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `z-ai/glm-5.2` | **5/5** | **$0.00014** | 93–381 | 1237–1310 |
| `deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro` | 5/6 | $0.00011 | 117–544 | 944–1216 |
| `moonshotai/kimi-k3` | 3/3 | $0.00556 | 55–117 | 0, 1536, 1536 |
| `qwen/qwen3.8-max` | 3/3 | $0.00598 | 259–710 | 0, 1024, 1024 |

**~40× cheaper than the outgoing deep model.** `deepseek-v4-pro` is marginally
cheaper still but produced one malformed-JSON response in six runs, which for a
lane is a failed call and a silent fallback — so it sits in the fallback chain
rather than in front.

`qwen3.8-max` was evaluated and rejected: cheaper per token than `kimi-k3` on
the rate card ($2/$6 against $3/$15) but it reasons 3–6× more, which spends the
difference and then some.

## Where the bill actually came from

The live figure worth anchoring on is PR #62's `security` lane: **$0.2614 for
82,914 input and 842 output tokens**. Almost all input. So the deep model's
**$3.00/M input rate** was the cost, not its output rate and not reasoning —
which was disabled in production anyway.

At $0.07/M input, the same call is roughly $0.006. That is the change; picking a
model with a cheaper *output* rate would have moved almost nothing.

## Reasoning is on again, and it was measured

It was hard-disabled for a real reason, kept verbatim in the code: reasoning is
billed against the same `max_tokens` as the answer, and `kimi-k3` on a 49k-token
prompt spent all 8000 completion tokens thinking and returned **empty** content
— `finish_reason: length`, 17k characters of reasoning. A
`reasoning: {max_tokens: 4096}` cap did not hold; it ran to 37k characters.

GLM 5.2 at `high`: 93–381 reasoning tokens against an 8000 ceiling, `stop` every
time, valid structured output every time.

`models.reasoning_effort = "off"` restores the old behaviour outright, because a
model whose reasoning eats the answer is not fixed by asking it to think less.
`"max"` was tried and is **not** recommended: it is undocumented, passed through
rather than validated, and produced malformed JSON on one of two attempts.

## The fallback chain was a guaranteed failure

Found while running issue triage on this repository. When the primary hit a
credit limit, the first fallback `moonshotai/kimi-k2.7-code` returned:

```
HTTP 400: Reasoning is mandatory for this endpoint and cannot be disabled.
```

Reasoning was disabled globally, so **that fallback could never succeed**, and
the second failed identically. Any primary-model problem was fatal rather than
degraded — the opposite of a fallback chain's purpose. Both replacements were
tested against the reasoning setting actually in force.

## Both tiers are the same model, and the two keys stay separate

`scan` and `deep` both point at GLM 5.2, but they remain two keys because the
shape of the decision is worth keeping: `scan` is mechanical work run often,
`deep` reads code closely. A deployment wanting a stronger deep tier changes one
line — and `defaults.toml` now states what that costs, so nobody raises it
without seeing the bill.

## Verification

- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `cargo clippy --locked --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo test --locked` — 981 passed; `--all-features` — 1,122 passed, 0 failed
- Prices for every model named here added to `harness::pricing`, so cost
  accounting and the budget ceiling keep working; an unpriced model still fails
  closed.
- Every figure above is a measurement against the live API.

+    fn every_model_the_defaults_select_has_a_price() {
+        // The test that matters more than any individual row. `completion_cost`

+        let cost = completion_cost("z-ai/glm-5.2", 82_914, 0, 842);

+            (0.005..0.007).contains(&cost),

+        );
+    }
+

+    fn a_cached_read_is_charged_at_the_cache_rate() {
+        // GLM 5.2 reads cache at a fifth of its input price, and a re-review is
+        // mostly cache. Charging cached tokens at full price would misreport
+        // exactly the number this change exists to move.
+        let cold = completion_cost("z-ai/glm-5.2", 100_000, 0, 1_000);
+        let warm = completion_cost("z-ai/glm-5.2", 100_000, 90_000, 1_000);
+
+        assert!(
+            warm < cold,
+            "cached tokens must cost less: {warm} vs {cold}"
+        );
+    }
+
+    #[test]
+    fn the_middle_argument_is_cached_tokens_not_output() {
+        // Every parameter is a `u64`, so swapping two of them compiles and
+        // silently misreports the bill. Output is priced far above cache reads,
+        // so the two orderings are distinguishable — which is what this asserts.
+        let correct = completion_cost("z-ai/glm-5.2", 1_000_000, 0, 1_000_000);
+        let swapped = completion_cost("z-ai/glm-5.2", 1_000_000, 1_000_000, 0);
+
+        assert!(
+            correct > swapped,
+            "input+output must cost more than input-all-cached: {correct} vs {swapped}"
+        );
+    }

+        // writing this test, which is why the ordering is now pinned below.
+        let cost = completion_cost("z-ai/glm-5.2", 82_914, 0, 842);
+
+        assert!(
+            (0.005..0.007).contains(&cost),
+            "expected roughly $0.006 for the 83k-token security call, got {cost:.5}"
+        );
+    }
+
+    #[test]
+    fn a_cached_read_is_charged_at_the_cache_rate() {
+        // GLM 5.2 reads cache at a fifth of its input price, and a re-review is
+        // mostly cache. Charging cached tokens at full price would misreport
+        // exactly the number this change exists to move.
+        let cold = completion_cost("z-ai/glm-5.2", 100_000, 0, 1_000);
+        let warm = completion_cost("z-ai/glm-5.2", 100_000, 90_000, 1_000);
+
+        assert!(
+            warm < cold,
+            "cached tokens must cost less: {warm} vs {cold}"
+        );
+    }
+
+    #[test]
+    fn the_middle_argument_is_cached_tokens_not_output() {
+        // Every parameter is a `u64`, so swapping two of them compiles and
+        // silently misreports the bill. Output is priced far above cache reads,
+        // so the two orderings are distinguishable — which is what this asserts.
+        let correct = completion_cost("z-ai/glm-5.2", 1_000_000, 0, 1_000_000);
+        let swapped = completion_cost("z-ai/glm-5.2", 1_000_000, 1_000_000, 0);
+
+        assert!(
+            correct > swapped,
+            "input+output must cost more than input-all-cached: {correct} vs {swapped}"
+        );
+    }
 }

comments.body:
The `description` lane read a body I had already replaced — I pushed the commit and edited the body a minute later, so the webhook fired on the old text. Against what it saw, all three findings were correct.

The third one survives the body update and was worth fixing: **`qwen/qwen3.8-max` had a price entry and no basis** — nothing selects it.

Rather than delete it, I stated why unused entries exist, because the reason is load-bearing:

> Entries exist for models this deployment does not currently select. That is deliberate: `completion_cost` fails closed on an unpriced model, so a one-line change to `models.deep` would otherwise take the budget ceiling with it. Every model here was measured before being priced.

Each unused entry now carries its verdict too — `qwen3.8-max` is marked as evaluated and rejected, with the measurement that decided it ($0.00598 a call against `kimi-k3`'s $0.00556, because it reasons 3–6× more).

The first two findings are the stale-body ones. The body now matches the diff: GLM 5.2 on both tiers, priced and measured, with the fallback chain as written.

Worth noting what happened here in general terms: an accurate reviewer plus a body edited after the push produces a confident, well-argued, wrong review. The lane is doing its job — a diff-versus-description check is exactly the kind of thing that catches a body someone forgot to update — it just cannot see an edit that arrives after it ran.

comments.author: senamakel
comments.body:
Both findings were right, and acting on the first one **found a bug in the test I was writing to satisfy it** — which is the best possible outcome for a "this is untested" finding.

`completion_cost(model, input, cached, output)`. I called it `(model, input, output, cached)`. Every parameter is a `u64`, so it compiled, ran, and silently misreported the bill — the cached call came out **four times more expensive** than the cold one. That is exactly the failure mode the price table exists to prevent, and nothing would have caught it.

So the ordering is now pinned by a test of its own, `the_middle_argument_is_cached_tokens_not_output`, which works because output is priced far above cache reads and the two orderings are therefore distinguishable.

Five tests added:

- **`every_model_the_defaults_select_has_a_price`** — the one that matters most. It parses the shipped `defaults.toml` and asserts `scan`, `deep` and every fallback are priced. `completion_cost` fails closed on an unpriced model, so naming one in defaults turns the budget ceiling into a hard error on the first review of the day — in production, not in CI. This is now a compile-and-test-time failure instead.
- **`the_new_deep_tier_costs_what_the_table_says`** — anchored on the real figure this change was made against: PR #62's security lane, 82,914 input and 842 output tokens, $0.2614 on the outgoing model. Asserts ~$0.006 here.
- **`a_cached_read_is_charged_at_the_cache_rate`** — a re-review is mostly cache, and charging it at full input price would misreport precisely the number this change exists to move.
- **`the_middle_argument_is_cached_tokens_not_output`** — above.
- **`the_configured_effort_reaches_the_gateway`** — the second finding. Asserts the wire between config and gateway rather than just `reasoning_options` in isolation, because that is the half that leaves a setting inert. `max_tokens` had exactly this bug: read, validated, documented, never forwarded.

985 passing, 1,127 with all features.

comments.body:
Pushing back on the `description` finding: **the mismatch it reports does not exist.**

Body:

```
| `fallback` | `kimi-k2.7-code`, `minimax-m2.1` | `deepseek-v4-pro`, `minimax-m3` |
```

Diff:

```
+fallback = ["deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro", "minimax/minimax-m3"]
```

Those agree. The title is `perf(models): move to GLM 5.2, and make reasoning configurable`, and the diff sets both tiers to `z-ai/glm-5.2`. Those agree too.

This was a real finding two pushes ago, when I edited the body after pushing and the lane reviewed the old text. It has been fixed since, and the summary itself says **"(5 earlier finding(s) still open)"** — so the lane is not re-deriving it, it is **carrying it forward**.

That is worth treating as a defect rather than noise, because it is the failure mode the continuity design is most exposed to: prior findings are replayed into the prompt so a re-review stays cheap and consistent, and the risk is that the model agrees with them instead of re-checking them against the current diff. A finding that cannot be retired by fixing it is worse than one that was never raised — it trains everyone to ignore the lane.

Filing it separately. The `tests` lane, by contrast, correctly noticed its earlier findings were addressed and said so in its summary — so the retirement path works there, which makes the `description` behaviour a bug rather than a missing feature.

Merging on the strength of the evidence above.

# Repository Guidelines

## Project Structure & Module Organization

- `src/` — the single crate. One responsibility per module, core types in a
  module-local `types.rs`, and every port in `src/ports/` is one trait in one
  file.
- `src/bin/tinysweeper.rs` — the CLI. Every subcommand is declared even when its
  milestone has not landed, so scripts and runbooks can be written against a
  stable surface. `src/server/` is the only production surface: tinysweeper is
  not distributed or run as a GitHub Action. The single, deliberate exception is
  `.github/workflows/manual-review.yml` in *this* repository — an operator
  button that POSTs to the deployed server's `/admin/reviews` route. It builds
  nothing, runs no lane, and holds no model or write credential; anything that
  would need one belongs in `src/server/`, not in a workflow.
- `presets/` — review policy as **data**, not code. A preset is a folder with a
  `preset.toml`, a `README.md`, and optional prompt overrides. Adding a preset
  is a new folder, never a new module.
- `vendor/tinyagents` — the agent harness, as a git submodule. Never edit it
  here; change it upstream and bump the pin.
- `docs/modules/<module>/README.md` — one document per `src/` module.
- `examples/` — declared explicitly in `Cargo.toml` with `required-features`, so
  credential-needing smoke tests never build in CI.

## Build, Test, and Development Commands

```sh
git submodule update --init --recursive
cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo clippy --locked --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo test --locked
cargo check --locked --all-features --all-targets
```

The default build is offline: it links no HTTP client and the test suite never
touches the network. Anything that needs the network goes behind a feature
(`harness`, `github`, `serve`).

## Coding Style & Naming Conventions

- rustfmt output, Rust 2024 idioms. `snake_case` modules and files,
  `PascalCase` types.
- Return `Result<T>` using the crate error type from `src/error.rs`.
- Every file opens with a `//!` module doc describing its role and any feature
  gating.
- Comments explain the *decision*, not the code. When a flag or an ordering is
  load-bearing, say so and say why.
- Public items carry doc comments. Clap fields use `///` — it becomes the help
  text.

## Testing Guidelines

- Tests live **in-crate**: a `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` block at the bottom of the
  module, moving to a sibling `test.rs` or `<name>_test.rs` when they grow.
  There is no `tests/` directory.
- Every port has an always-compiled offline mock. `MockForge` records what would
  have been written so tests can assert on exact check runs and comments.
- Lane behaviour is covered by golden tests: fixture diff plus a canned
  structured model response, asserting the findings that survive filtering,
  dedupe and capping. These are the tests that keep noise control honest.
- Maintain at least 80% coverage for meaningful library behaviour.

## Documentation Expectations

Keep every Markdown file, including this one, at 500 lines or fewer. When a
topic grows past that limit, split it into focused files and link them from the
module's `README.md`.

## Security Boundary

These are invariants, not preferences. Changing any of them needs an explicit
discussion in the pull request:

- The model never holds a write token. Lanes run against a read-only checkout;
  write credentials are minted only in `src/apply/`, after every model call has
  returned. A lane that leaves a change in the checkout fails.
- Contributor code is never executed. We read the diff and the tree; we do not
  build, install dependencies, or run the target repository's scripts.
- Pull request bodies, comments and diffs are untrusted input. Fence and label
  them as data in prompts. A model verdict is advisory — only deterministic
  policy in `src/apply/` and `src/automerge/` may mutate GitHub.
- Secrets found by the scanners are reported by type and location only. The
  value never reaches a comment, a check-run summary, or a log.

## Commit & Pull Request Guidelines

Use concise, imperative commit subjects. Keep commits small; commit each
coherent, validated slice on its own. Pull requests state what changed, any
behaviour change, and how it was verified.
